Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The Wa State Central Economic Planning Commission first announced on April 15, 2023, that all mining and excavation of mineral resources would be suspended effective August 1, 2023. Wa State is the primary source of tin imported by China, the world's largest producer of refined tin, and the International Tin Association (ITA) estimates the halt affects about 10% of the world's tin concentrate supply. The stated reason for the ban is to protect the remaining mineral resources and implement more mature mining regulations and monitoring. The news of the suspension caused a significant market reaction, with tin prices on the London Metal Exchange rising. The halt on operations, which included a ban on ore transport, was expected to be more prolonged than initially anticipated. <2> In a notice issued on April 15, 2023, the Central Economic Commission of Burma's self-administered Wa State announced a suspension of all mining and processing operations, effective August 1, 2023, to conduct an audit and conserve mineral resources. [4, 5, 6] This indefinite halt on all exploration, mining, and processing activities impacted the global tin market, as Wa State is a significant supplier, accounting for about 10% of the world's tin concentrate. [4] The announcement led to a surge in tin prices due to supply concerns, with the London Metal Exchange 3-month price increasing by 9%. [4] [3, 5] [3, 5] <3> The U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) made a preliminary determination that there is a reasonable indication that the U.S. tin mill products industry is materially injured by imports from Canada, China, Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. These imports are allegedly subsidized by the government of China and sold in the United States at less than fair value. This affirmative determination, voted on by Chairman David S. Johanson and Commissioners Rhonda K. Schmidtlein, Jason E. Kearns, Randolph J. Stayin, and Amy A. Karpel, means the U.S. Department of Commerce will proceed with its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations. The downward revision, detailed in a report published on March 9, 2023, was attributed to several factors including a strengthening US dollar, a slow demand recovery in China, weakening global macroeconomic fundamentals, and high global inflation. The report also noted that tin prices were expected to remain under pressure during the first half of 2023, influenced by a slowing global economy and an increase in global tin stocks since June 2022. <5> On January 18, 2023, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. and the United Steelworkers (USW) union filed petitions with the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC). [9, 10, 12] The petitions called for antidumping and countervailing duty investigations into what they allege are unfairly traded imports of tin and chromium coated sheet steel products, collectively known as tin mill products. [9, 13, 14] The countries accused of dumping these products—selling them at less than fair value—are Canada, China, Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. [9, 10] A countervailing duty investigation was also requested for China, alleging that its government subsidizes the production of these goods. [9, 10] The petitioners claim that this unfair trade has caused material injury to the U.S. steel industry. [11] Notice of the institution of these investigations was published in the Federal Register on January 24, 2023.

metadata.original_text: This time series records tin USD T data in the Commodity market price domain, with a collection frequency of daily, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2023-11-30 to 2023-12-15. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A market analysis of the third quarter of 2023 confirms that US economic uncertainty, particularly surrounding future monetary policy, negatively impacted tin and other industrial metal prices. In its meeting on September 20, 2023, the US Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decided to maintain the target federal funds rate at a range of 5.25% to 5.5%. While this was a pause in interest rate hikes, the accompanying commentary was considered hawkish. Officials projected the possibility of another rate increase before the end of the year and indicated that rates might need to remain higher for longer than previously anticipated to effectively combat inflation. This stance created concern in the markets that sustained higher interest rates could slow economic growth, thereby reducing future demand for industrial metals like tin. This bearish sentiment contributed to price volatility for metals during the quarter. <2> Through Decree No. 296.K/MB.01/MEM.B/2023, Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) officially classified 47 minerals, including tin, as critical. [1] This strategic move is aimed at securing the domestic supply of raw materials for strategic industries, strengthening national defense and security, and promoting sustainable resource management. [1, 4] The classification is expected to serve as a reference for the governance of the entire mineral-based industrial chain, from upstream to downstream, including the processing and refining of residues. The government emphasized that this designation will guide policies on trade, fiscal matters, and the prioritization of minerals for domestic needs, potentially leading to a simplification of the industry's legal framework and enhanced processing methods. [4] <3> The Wa State Central Economic Planning Commission first announced on April 15, 2023, that all mining and excavation of mineral resources would be suspended effective August 1, 2023. The suspension was implemented as planned, halting all mining and processing operations in the region, which is a significant global source of tin. Wa State is the primary source of tin imported by China, the world's largest producer of refined tin, and the International Tin Association (ITA) estimates the halt affects about 10% of the world's tin concentrate supply. The stated reason for the ban is to protect the remaining mineral resources and implement more mature mining regulations and monitoring. The news of the suspension caused a significant market reaction, with tin prices on the London Metal Exchange rising. The halt on operations, which included a ban on ore transport, was expected to be more prolonged than initially anticipated. <4> In a notice issued on April 15, 2023, the Central Economic Commission of Burma's self-administered Wa State announced a suspension of all mining and processing operations, effective August 1, 2023, to conduct an audit and conserve mineral resources. [4, 5, 6] This indefinite halt on all exploration, mining, and processing activities impacted the global tin market, as Wa State is a significant supplier, accounting for about 10% of the world's tin concentrate. [4] The announcement led to a surge in tin prices due to supply concerns, with the London Metal Exchange 3-month price increasing by 9%. [4] Following the August 1st shutdown, all mines, processing plants, and ore transport ceased, and inspections were implemented to enforce the suspension. [3, 5] While there was an existing stockpile of raw ore, the closure of processing plants prevented it from being sold. [3, 5] <5> The U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) made a preliminary determination that there is a reasonable indication that the U.S. tin mill products industry is materially injured by imports from Canada, China, Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. These imports are allegedly subsidized by the government of China and sold in the United States at less than fair value. This affirmative determination, voted on by Chairman David S. Johanson and Commissioners Rhonda K. Schmidtlein, Jason E. Kearns, Randolph J. Stayin, and Amy A. Karpel, means the U.S. Department of Commerce will proceed with its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations. The petitions prompting the investigation were filed on January 18, 2023, by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. and the United Steel, Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial and Service Workers International Union. <6> Fitch Solutions revised its 2023 tin price forecast down to $20,000 per tonne, a significant drop from the 2022 average of $30,959 per tonne. The downward revision, detailed in a report published on March 9, 2023, was attributed to several factors including a strengthening US dollar, a slow demand recovery in China, weakening global macroeconomic fundamentals, and high global inflation. The report also noted that tin prices were expected to remain under pressure during the first half of 2023, influenced by a slowing global economy and an increase in global tin stocks since June 2022. <7> On January 18, 2023, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. and the United Steelworkers (USW) union filed petitions with the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC). [9, 10, 12] The petitions called for antidumping and countervailing duty investigations into what they allege are unfairly traded imports of tin and chromium coated sheet steel products, collectively known as tin mill products. [9, 13, 14] The countries accused of dumping these products—selling them at less than fair value—are Canada, China, Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. [9, 10] A countervailing duty investigation was also requested for China, alleging that its government subsidizes the production of these goods. [9, 10] The petitioners claim that this unfair trade has caused material injury to the U.S. steel industry. [11] Notice of the institution of these investigations was published in the Federal Register on January 24, 2023.

Prediction target period: from 2024-04-03 to 2024-04-18. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In its annual Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024 report, published on January 31, 2024, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) detailed domestic tin consumption for the 2023 calendar year. [1, 3] The report confirmed that the largest end uses for tin in the United States were tinplate at 23% and chemicals at 22%. [7] These were followed by alloys and solder, each accounting for 11% of consumption. [7] The comprehensive breakdown also included babbitt, brass and bronze, and tinning at 7%, bar tin at 2%, and other uses at 24%. [7] The report further noted that tin has not been mined in the U.S. since 1993 or smelted since 1989, with 25 firms consuming over 93% of the primary tin in 2023. [7] <2> A market analysis of the third quarter of 2023 confirms that US economic uncertainty, particularly surrounding future monetary policy, negatively impacted tin and other industrial metal prices. In its meeting on September 20, 2023, the US Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decided to maintain the target federal funds rate at a range of 5.25% to 5.5%. While this was a pause in interest rate hikes, the accompanying commentary was considered hawkish. Officials projected the possibility of another rate increase before the end of the year and indicated that rates might need to remain higher for longer than previously anticipated to effectively combat inflation. This stance created concern in the markets that sustained higher interest rates could slow economic growth, thereby reducing future demand for industrial metals like tin. This bearish sentiment contributed to price volatility for metals during the quarter. <3> Through Decree No. 296.K/MB.01/MEM.B/2023, Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) officially classified 47 minerals, including tin, as critical. [1] This strategic move is aimed at securing the domestic supply of raw materials for strategic industries, strengthening national defense and security, and promoting sustainable resource management. [1, 4] The classification is expected to serve as a reference for the governance of the entire mineral-based industrial chain, from upstream to downstream, including the processing and refining of residues. The government emphasized that this designation will guide policies on trade, fiscal matters, and the prioritization of minerals for domestic needs, potentially leading to a simplification of the industry's legal framework and enhanced processing methods. [4] <4> The Wa State Central Economic Planning Commission first announced on April 15, 2023, that all mining and excavation of mineral resources would be suspended effective August 1, 2023. The suspension was implemented as planned, halting all mining and processing operations in the region, which is a significant global source of tin. Wa State is the primary source of tin imported by China, the world's largest producer of refined tin, and the International Tin Association (ITA) estimates the halt affects about 10% of the world's tin concentrate supply. The stated reason for the ban is to protect the remaining mineral resources and implement more mature mining regulations and monitoring. The news of the suspension caused a significant market reaction, with tin prices on the London Metal Exchange rising. The halt on operations, which included a ban on ore transport, was expected to be more prolonged than initially anticipated. <5> In a notice issued on April 15, 2023, the Central Economic Commission of Burma's self-administered Wa State announced a suspension of all mining and processing operations, effective August 1, 2023, to conduct an audit and conserve mineral resources. [4, 5, 6] This indefinite halt on all exploration, mining, and processing activities impacted the global tin market, as Wa State is a significant supplier, accounting for about 10% of the world's tin concentrate. [4] The announcement led to a surge in tin prices due to supply concerns, with the London Metal Exchange 3-month price increasing by 9%. [4] Following the August 1st shutdown, all mines, processing plants, and ore transport ceased, and inspections were implemented to enforce the suspension. [3, 5] While there was an existing stockpile of raw ore, the closure of processing plants prevented it from being sold. [3, 5] <6> The U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC) made a preliminary determination that there is a reasonable indication that the U.S. tin mill products industry is materially injured by imports from Canada, China, Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. These imports are allegedly subsidized by the government of China and sold in the United States at less than fair value. This affirmative determination, voted on by Chairman David S. Johanson and Commissioners Rhonda K. Schmidtlein, Jason E. Kearns, Randolph J. Stayin, and Amy A. Karpel, means the U.S. Department of Commerce will proceed with its antidumping and countervailing duty investigations. The petitions prompting the investigation were filed on January 18, 2023, by Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. and the United Steel, Paper and Forestry, Rubber, Manufacturing, Energy, Allied Industrial and Service Workers International Union. <7> Fitch Solutions revised its 2023 tin price forecast down to $20,000 per tonne, a significant drop from the 2022 average of $30,959 per tonne. The downward revision, detailed in a report published on March 9, 2023, was attributed to several factors including a strengthening US dollar, a slow demand recovery in China, weakening global macroeconomic fundamentals, and high global inflation. The report also noted that tin prices were expected to remain under pressure during the first half of 2023, influenced by a slowing global economy and an increase in global tin stocks since June 2022. <8> On January 18, 2023, Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. and the United Steelworkers (USW) union filed petitions with the U.S. Department of Commerce and the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC). [9, 10, 12] The petitions called for antidumping and countervailing duty investigations into what they allege are unfairly traded imports of tin and chromium coated sheet steel products, collectively known as tin mill products. [9, 13, 14] The countries accused of dumping these products—selling them at less than fair value—are Canada, China, Germany, the Netherlands, South Korea, Taiwan, Turkey, and the United Kingdom. [9, 10] A countervailing duty investigation was also requested for China, alleging that its government subsidizes the production of these goods. [9, 10] The petitioners claim that this unfair trade has caused material injury to the U.S. steel industry. [11] Notice of the institution of these investigations was published in the Federal Register on January 24, 2023.

metadata.original_text: This time series records tin USD T data in the Commodity market price domain, with a collection frequency of daily, focusing on monitoring and analyzing relevant indicators. Prediction target period: from 2024-11-13 to 2024-11-28. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> The International Tin Association (ITA) released the findings of its 20th annual survey of global tin users on October 30, 2024. The survey, conducted between June and September 2024, gathered data from 80 companies which account for approximately 42% of the world's refined tin consumption in 2023. The results forecast a 3.0% increase in tin demand for 2024, to 367,900 tonnes, suggesting the industry is entering a moderate recovery cycle driven by China and supported by technology. <2> A report from the International Tin Association (ITA) indicated that a downturn in the residential construction sectors in both the U.S. and China negatively impacted the tin chemicals market during 2023. This macroeconomic trend contributed to a 3.1% decrease in tin use for chemicals among the companies surveyed for the year. <3> On September 2, 2024, BMI, a unit of Fitch Solutions, announced an upward revision of its average tin price forecast for 2024, increasing it from $28,000 to $30,000 per tonne. This adjustment is attributed to dual pressures of supply constraints and rising demand. The supply side is impacted by ongoing disruptions in key producing nations, Myanmar and Indonesia. Simultaneously, demand from the electronics sector is strengthening, evidenced by a pickup in global semiconductor sales from Taiwan, continued Chinese investment in its domestic chip manufacturing capacity, and Japan's renewed focus on bolstering its own manufacturing. <4> On July 12, 2024, the U.S. Department of Commerce's International Trade Administration issued a proposed rule to update its regulations concerning antidumping (AD) and countervailing (CVD) duties. [4, 5] The proposal aims to enhance the administration of trade remedy laws by codifying and revising procedures. [1] Key areas addressed include the collection of cash deposits, the application of AD rates in nonmarket economy proceedings, and the attribution of subsidies for cross-owned companies. [2, 4] This regulatory update, which could impact future import costs, is open for a public comment period, with written comments due by September 10, 2024, to be considered. [1, 4] <5> In its annual Mineral Commodity Summaries 2024 report, published on January 31, 2024, the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS) detailed domestic tin consumption for the 2023 calendar year. [1, 3] The report confirmed that the largest end uses for tin in the United States were tinplate at 23% and chemicals at 22%. [7] These were followed by alloys and solder, each accounting for 11% of consumption. [7] The comprehensive breakdown also included babbitt, brass and bronze, and tinning at 7%, bar tin at 2%, and other uses at 24%. [7] The report further noted that tin has not been mined in the U.S. since 1993 or smelted since 1989, with 25 firms consuming over 93% of the primary tin in 2023. [7] <6> A market analysis of the third quarter of 2023 confirms that US economic uncertainty, particularly surrounding future monetary policy, negatively impacted tin and other industrial metal prices. In its meeting on September 20, 2023, the US Federal Reserve's Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) decided to maintain the target federal funds rate at a range of 5.25% to 5.5%. While this was a pause in interest rate hikes, the accompanying commentary was considered hawkish. Officials projected the possibility of another rate increase before the end of the year and indicated that rates might need to remain higher for longer than previously anticipated to effectively combat inflation. This stance created concern in the markets that sustained higher interest rates could slow economic growth, thereby reducing future demand for industrial metals like tin. This bearish sentiment contributed to price volatility for metals during the quarter. <7> Through Decree No. 296.K/MB.01/MEM.B/2023, Indonesia's Ministry of Energy and Mineral Resources (ESDM) officially classified 47 minerals, including tin, as critical. [1] This strategic move is aimed at securing the domestic supply of raw materials for strategic industries, strengthening national defense and security, and promoting sustainable resource management. [1, 4] The classification is expected to serve as a reference for the governance of the entire mineral-based industrial chain, from upstream to downstream, including the processing and refining of residues. The government emphasized that this designation will guide policies on trade, fiscal matters, and the prioritization of minerals for domestic needs, potentially leading to a simplification of the industry's legal framework and enhanced processing methods. [4] <8> The Wa State Central Economic Planning Commission first announced on April 15, 2023, that all mining and excavation of mineral resources would be suspended effective August 1, 2023. The suspension was implemented as planned, halting all mining and processing operations in the region, which is a significant global source of tin. Wa State is the primary source of tin imported by China, the world's largest producer of refined tin, and the International Tin Association (ITA) estimates the halt affects about 10% of the world's tin concentrate supply. The stated reason for the ban is to protect the remaining mineral resources and implement more mature mining regulations and monitoring. The news of the suspension caused a significant market reaction, with tin prices on the London Metal Exchange rising. The halt on operations, which included a ban on ore transport, was expected to be more prolonged than initially anticipated. <9> In a notice issued on April 15, 2023, the Central Economic Commission of Burma's self-administered Wa State announced a suspension of all mining and processing operations, effective August 1, 2023, to conduct an audit and conserve mineral resources. [4, 5, 6] This indefinite halt on all exploration, mining, and processing activities impacted the global tin market, as Wa State is a significant supplier, accounting for about 10% of the world's tin concentrate. [4] The announcement led to a surge in tin prices due to supply concerns, with the London Metal Exchange 3-month price increasing by 9%. [4] Following the August 1st shutdown, all mines, processing plants, and ore transport ceased, and inspections were implemented to enforce the suspension. [3, 5] While there was an existing stockpile of raw ore, the closure of processing plants prevented it from being sold. [3, 5]
